source: Panickssery, Bowman, Feng (2024) LLM Evaluators Recognize and Favor Their Own Generations
finding: LLM judges can tell their own text from others and favour it. Fine-tuning for self-recognition raises self-preference in a straight line. This is the mechanism behind the same-family judge problem (gap 7).
numbers: Out of the box GPT-3.5, GPT-4 and Llama 2 all beat 50% at spotting own output; GPT-4 73.5% when picking itself against two other LLMs and humans. Fine-tuned GPT-3.5 and Llama 2 over 90% self-recognition after 500 examples. Self-preference strength is linear in self-recognition (Fig 1). Tasks: CNN/DailyMail and XSUM summaries.
quote: LLMs such as GPT-4 and Llama 2 have non-trivial accuracy at distinguishing themselves from other LLMs and humans.
limits: Summarisation, not novelty rating. Correlation shown by fine-tuning; the causal claim is argued, not proven. Weak models cannot spot stronger ones (Llama 2 cannot tell itself from GPT-3.5 or GPT-4).
agent_relevance: Do not let the generating model family also grade novelty of its own candidates. Use a judge from another family, or blind and shuffle the sources.

source: Wataoka, Takahashi, Ri (2024/2025) Self-Preference Bias in LLM-as-a-Judge
finding: Eight LLM judges compared with human votes on Chatbot Arena pairs. GPT-4 shows the largest self-preference. Judges also give higher marks to lower-perplexity text, whoever wrote it, which is a likely cause.
numbers: GPT-4 self-preference score 0.520 (recall 0.945 vs 0.425 between the two human-preference cases). Vicuna-13b and Koala-13b next; other models near zero. Most judges (not stablelm-tuned-alpha-7b, dolly-v2-12b) gave higher ratings to lower-perplexity responses than humans did.
limits: Dialogue answers, not research ideas or novelty. Human votes are the gold. Perplexity link is correlational.
agent_relevance: Judge scores for novelty may reward familiar, fluent text, the opposite of novelty. Low perplexity under the judge is a bias to control for (gaps 2 and 7).

source: Si, Hashimoto, Yang (2025) The Ideation-Execution Gap, Appendix D (ideation vs execution score correlation)
finding: Reviewer scores given before execution barely predict scores after execution. For AI ideas the link is weak and for excitement it is moderately negative. So a pre-commit rating by readers is not a reliable check on the drop (gap 4).
numbers: N=43 executed projects. AI ideas after execution score below human ideas on all four metrics (excitement 3.90 vs 4.48, effectiveness 4.13 vs 4.78), not significant at N=43. Table 9 (extraction garbled, read with care): AI novelty r about -0.02, AI excitement Pearson r -0.321, Spearman -0.386; human correlations between about -0.15 and 0.21. Change in overall score tracks change in novelty, excitement and effectiveness; overall vs effectiveness r=0.654.
quote: the correlation is weak in most cases; and for AI ideas, there is even a moderately negative correlation on the excitement score.
limits: Small N, NLP prompting ideas only, human executors who may change the idea. Table text was garbled, so exact cell assignment is uncertain.
agent_relevance: A scaffold cannot trust a pre-execution novelty score. Add a cheap execution or verification step and rate novelty again afterwards.

source: Wen, Si, Chen, He, Feng (2025) Predicting Empirical AI Research Outcomes with Language Models
finding: A fine-tuned model with a retrieval agent can predict which of two ideas will perform better after execution, far better than experts and than frontier models alone. This is a trained pre-commit check, but for effectiveness, not novelty.
numbers: 1,585 test idea pairs (6,000 training pairs), 25 human experts. NLP domain: system 64.4% vs experts 48.9%. Full test set 77%. Off-the-shelf frontier LMs such as o3 near random even with the same retrieval. On unpublished AI-generated ideas 63.6%.
limits: Needs fine-tuning on 6,000 pairs; the target is a benchmark win, not novelty. A scaffold-only agent has no such trained predictor.
agent_relevance: Retrieval alone did not rescue a frontier model here, so gap 3 needs a task-specific test, not an assumption. A learned check on outcome may beat a novelty rating.

source: Chen, Tong, Wu et al. (2025) Beyond Brainstorming: What Drives High-Quality Scientific Ideas? Lessons from Multi-Agent Collaboration
finding: Multi-agent discussion beats a single agent with self-reflection on LLM-scored proposal quality. A leader helps. Diverse teams help; a team of only junior agents does not. Gains flatten beyond 3 agents.
numbers: Generator DeepSeek-V3; judges Qwen3-32B and o1-mini (different families from the generator). 20 topics x 50 seeds = 1,000 proposals per question (about 7,000 overall). Overall score +0.46 (Qwen3) and +0.44 (o1-mini) over solo. Leader: overall +0.57 (Qwen3) over solo. Interdisciplinary and mixed-seniority teams best; all-junior team OA 7.73 vs solo 7.75. Five agents or over 8 rounds: minimal gain. Longer discussion raises novelty but lowers workability. Human blind A/B on 40 pairs: multi-agent preferred 87.5% (p<0.01).
limits: Not equal tokens (multi-agent uses more calls). Human check only 40 proposals by two graduate students. No distinct-k; novelty is a judge rating. Closest thing to gap 6 but not a diversity measurement.
agent_relevance: Mixed personas with a leader that integrates may be worth testing against a single sampled pool at equal tokens. Keep the group small (3).

source: Hope, Chan, Kittur, Shahaf (2017) Accelerating Innovation Through Analogy Mining (KDD)
finding: A direct test of the Uzzi pattern in a design task: inspirations near in purpose but far in mechanism gave more good ideas than same-domain (TF-IDF) near ones or random far ones.
numbers: Within-subjects, 749 ideas, 9 seeds common to all conditions. Good ideas (at least 2 of 5 judges): 46% (N=105) analogy vs 37% (N=49) random vs 30% (N=54) TF-IDF, p<=.01. Strict (3 of 5): 38% vs 22% vs 21%. Mixed model pr(good) 0.71 [0.48, 0.87] vs 0.28 [0.16, 0.44] TF-IDF vs 0.27 [0.16, 0.41] random; likelihood ratio chi2(3)=67.96. Judge agreement Fleiss kappa 0.51.
limits: Human crowd workers, product redesign, wide confidence intervals (authors say so). 'Far' means mechanism, tuned by the authors, not a measured threshold.
agent_relevance: Best direct support for gap 1: give the agent a near-purpose, far-mechanism element rather than all-near or all-random. Needs a test with LLM agents.

source: Hope, Tamari, Kang, Hershcovich, Chan, Kittur, Shahaf (2021/2022) Scaling Creative Inspiration with Fine-Grained Functional Aspects of Ideas
finding: Searching ideas by purpose and mechanism spans gives inspirations raters call useful. The authors note nearest-span results beat a looser method, perhaps by balancing too far against too near.
numbers: User study: BERT-based method 51% of individual inspirations rated useful (by at least 2 raters) vs best baseline under 30%; coherent boxes 62% vs 39% for best baseline. Rater agreement 50% by Fleiss kappa and Krippendorff alpha. Retrieval MAP 85 to 87%.
limits: Rater agreement is low. The too-far-or-near remark is a guess by the authors, not a tested threshold.
agent_relevance: Weak support for a distance sweet spot (gap 8). No threshold located.

source: Jiang et al. (2025) Artificial Hivemind: The Open-Ended Homogeneity of Language Models
finding: Many different models give similar answers to open prompts, so pooling models does not give much real diversity. Aggressive sampling does not fix it.
numbers: Inter-model pairwise similarity 71% to 82%; DeepSeek-V3 vs qwen-max 0.82, DeepSeek-V3 vs gpt-4o 0.81. Min-p sampling at temperature 2.0: 81% of response pairs still above 0.7 similarity and 61.2% above 0.8. 25 models detailed (70+ studied).
limits: Embedding similarity, not human novelty rating; open-ended chat prompts, not research ideas.
agent_relevance: A multi-sample or multi-model pool (gap 6) starts from a narrow base. Test distinct-k gain per token before counting on it.

source: Zhang et al. (2025) NoveltyBench: Evaluating Language Models for Humanlike Diversity (COLM)
finding: Models give fewer distinct answers than people. Bigger models in a family are often less diverse. Asking for creativity or paraphrasing the prompt barely helps; showing the model its earlier answers (in-context regeneration) roughly reaches human-writer diversity.
numbers: 1,100 prompts (100 curated with 8 human answers each, 1,000 from real chats), 20 models. In-context regeneration: three tested models roughly match human writers; GPT-4o and Gemini 2.0 Pro even exceed human cumulative utility. Paraphrase and system prompts: marginal.
quote: In-context regeneration is the most successful approach, with all three models roughly matching the diversity of human writers
limits: Diversity judged by functional-equivalence classes trained on 1,100 annotated pairs; human baseline is 8 authors at one institution, an approximate lower bound.
agent_relevance: For gap 6, sequential generation with prior answers in context is a cheap diversity step. Measure with equivalence classes, not n-gram overlap.

source: Lu et al. (2025) Benchmarking Language Model Creativity: A Case Study on Code Generation (NAACL)
finding: Solution-path novelty in code: forbid the techniques already used and ask again (Denial Prompting). Correct-and-new rates fall fast as constraints grow. Reasoning scaffolds mostly improve correctness, not divergence.
numbers: 199 Codeforces problems, 30 correct human solutions each (5.9K). Convergent creativity falls sharply with each added constraint for humans and LLMs. Of four reasoning strategies, only MCTS raised divergent creativity (all 5 states), with near-zero gain in the joint score after state 2; self-correction and planning raised convergent but cut divergent. GPT-4 was best but below humans.
limits: Code only; novelty = technique not in the 30 human solutions, so it depends on that set. Strategies were tested on different models (MCTS on CodeGemma-7B, others on GPT-3.5).
agent_relevance: Direct support for gap 9: path novelty can be measured against a set of known solution paths. Verification-style scaffolds may trade novelty for correctness.

source: Ye, Gu, Zhao, Yin, Wang (2024) Assessing the Creativity of LLMs in Proposing Novel Solutions to Mathematical Problems (CreativeMath)
finding: Given known solutions to a math problem, models must write a new correct one. Correct and novel is much rarer than correct alone for most models. High MATH accuracy does not predict novelty.
numbers: Gemini-1.5-Pro: Correctness Ratio 69.92%, Novelty Ratio 66.94%. Llama-3-70B novel/correct 82.87%. GPT-4o, DeepSeek-V2, Mixtral-8x22B: novel/correct under 50% despite similar correctness; GPT-4o 76.6% on MATH. Average novel-and-unknown to novel ratio about 95%. Sample sizes by number of reference solutions k=1..4: 400, 154, 42, 8.
limits: Correctness and novelty judged by three LLM evaluators (GPT-4, Claude 3.5 Sonnet, Gemini 1.5 Pro); no human gold seen in the parts read. Few cases at k=3 and 4.
agent_relevance: Gives a path-novelty test bed for maths-type tasks (gap 9). Judge agreement should be checked first.

source: Ruan et al. (2024/2026) LiveIdeaBench: Evaluating LLMs' Divergent Thinking for Scientific Idea Generation with Minimal Context
finding: Idea originality across 40+ models is only weakly tied to general intelligence scores. So being a strong solver does not mean being a novel one.
numbers: 1,180 keywords, 22 domains, 40+ models. Correlation with LiveBench general score r=0.357, p=0.038, r2=0.127, 95% CI [0.022, 0.621] (41 models). Same-family pairs differ: qwq-32b vs qwq-32b-preview similar creativity, very different general scores.
limits: Judged by a dynamic panel of LLMs; no human gold in the part read. CI almost touches zero.
agent_relevance: Gap 7: a judge panel from mixed families is a cheap hedge against same-family favouring. Do not infer novelty from capability.

source: Shibayama, Yin, Matsumoto (2021) Measuring novelty in science with word embedding (PLOS ONE 16(7): e0254034)
finding: An embedding-distance novelty score is checked against authors' own newness ratings, not expert tags. Correlation is small but positive. The paper does not test against Uzzi-style journal pairs. A correction was issued January 2026.
numbers: Questionnaire of 2,081 scientists (321 biomedical), one article each from 2001-2006, 5-point scale. Title-based Novel100 correlates r=.170 (p<.01) with newness. 2,000 biomedical 2010 articles with citations to 2020 (about 1,000 top-1%, oversampled); example odds ratio 154 for top-1%. Distance validated on 100 authors, 1,600 documents, 21,908 pairs.
limits: Self-rated novelty, one field. Other coefficients were in tables I could not read. Content of the 2026 correction not read. Page text came through a summarising fetch tool, not the raw PDF.
agent_relevance: Gap 2: text-embedding distance has a small measured link to human newness (r=.17), similar in size to Bornmann's weak link for journal pairs. No cheap proxy is strong.

source: Uzzi, Mukherjee, Stringer, Jones (2013) Supplementary Online Material (null model and robustness)
finding: The SOM gives the null model and robustness checks behind the hit-rate result. The null model is a degree-preserving rewiring, run 10 times. The hit effect survives field fixed effects, a top-1% hit cut and reference-count controls, and peaks at about the 85th percentile of conventionality.
numbers: 17.9 million WoS papers. 10 synthetic instances of the whole citation network. Logistic regressions in 33 subsamples (11 median-conventionality bins x 3 team-size classes) with 243 subfield fixed effects; papers with at least 10 references. Tail cut at 1st, 5th, 10th or 20th percentile of z all significant; at the 30th percentile and beyond the link disappears. Top-1% hit definition looks extremely similar. Hit probability peaks near the 85th percentile of median conventionality.
limits: All within one database and period (mostly 1990s for hits). No effect size beyond the logistic results was read. Only 10 null networks. A local scratch copy of the SOM text was read this session.
agent_relevance: Gap 5 is only half closed: robustness inside WoS holds, but no outside-WoS replication was opened. For our agent the shape is a sharp left tail on a conventional core.

source: Kumar, Vincentius, Jordan, Anderson (2025) Human Creativity in the Age of LLMs: Randomized Experiments on Divergent and Convergent Thinking (CHI)
finding: People given LLM strategy lists later wrote less original and more similar ideas when working alone. Shows a possible cost of a shared scaffold on diversity.
numbers: 460 participants in the divergent-thinking experiment (1,100 across two experiments), 9,457 ideas. Test-phase originality Kruskal-Wallis H(2)=9.14, p=0.010; List of Strategies worse than no-LLM, Dunn p=0.009. Test-phase fluency not different (H=1.14, p=0.566). Strategy group produced more similar ideas as a group after LLM use stopped.
limits: Humans, Alternate Uses Test, small effect, group diversity simulated by sampling.
agent_relevance: Gap 6 context: a common scaffold may narrow what a group does; do not equate shared frames with diverse teams.

source: Veugelers & Wang (2019) Scientific novelty and technological impact (Research Policy 48, DOI 10.1016/j.respol.2019.01.019)
finding: Not opened: the publisher page returned 403. Only bibliographic metadata was confirmed through Crossref (title, DOI, year). No numbers can be claimed.
Not opened: the DOI redirected to a ScienceDirect page that returned 403. Whether the validity numbers changed is unknown.
limits: Closed access from this machine; Crossref was rate-limited when I tried to look up the corrected article.
